criteria.criterion: Run `cargo test -p xtask`. A test in xtask/src/site.rs renders the real firstmate study and asserts that no run of 6 or more normalised words from a term definition (yolo, green, red, in scope, places, home) appears anywhere else in the page text, so reworded copies are caught; it passes.
criteria.evidence: I ran `cargo test -p xtask`: 83 unit tests passed, including no_run_of_six_words_from_a_definition_is_repeated_elsewhere_on_the_page. The test renders real_study(), removes the Glossary <dd> and the Words used first <dd> for each of the six terms, and checks 6-word windows in the text between 'Start here' and 'Claims and sources'. From reading the base text, the base limits[6] shares the run 'a local only ship or a' with the place definition, so the test would fail on the base. Caveat: both copies of a term are treated as 'the definition' and removed before the check. So the verbatim second copy of red and in scope (see criterion 2) is never compared with the first. Paraphrases of the place rule elsewhere are also not caught (see findings).

criteria.criterion: Run `cargo test -p xtask`. A test in xtask/src/site.rs asserts each of yolo, green, red, in scope, places and home has exactly one definition on the rendered page and that every href="#term-..." has a matching id.
criteria.evidence: each_term_has_one_definition_and_every_term_link_resolves passes. It checks that every href="#term-..." has an id, and that `<dt id="term-{slug}">` appears once. But the page itself has two definitions for five of the six terms. intro.json start_terms (lines 37-42) render as `<dt>yolo</dt>`, `<dt>in scope</dt>`, `<dt>green</dt>`, `<dt>red</dt>` and `<dt>home</dt>` with full definitions in Words used first (start_here, site.rs:332-342). The Glossary (lines 98, 112, 121-123) defines them again. The red text (line 40 vs 122) and the in scope text (line 38 vs 98) are word-for-word identical. The home sentence 'A secondmate is a persistent home of its own' appears in both. The terms lead-in still says 'Each is defined here, and again in the Glossary'. The new test itself calls without_definition for both `<dt id=...>` and `<dt>{term}</dt>`, which admits there are two definitions. The assertion counts only Glossary ids, so it does not check the stated property. I read this from source because the rendered index.html is outside my working directory and my read was denied.

findings.summary: yolo, green, red, in scope and home are still defined twice on the page (Words used first and the Glossary), red and in scope word for word
findings.evidence: intro.json start_terms (lines 37-42) and glossary (lines 98, 112, 121-123) both define these terms. red is identical in both ('A PR that is failing, or has a required check that has not reported. It is not merged under either yolo setting...'), and so is in scope. 'A secondmate is a persistent home of its own' appears in both home entries. The terms lead-in still says 'Each is defined here, and again in the Glossary'. The original request said 'define each term ... in exactly one place, the Glossary or Words used first', and the accepted reading says 'once (Glossary or Words used first)'. The rejected attempt had removed these Glossary duplicates; this retry brings them back. Fix: keep one definition per term. For example, keep the Words used first entry and replace the Glossary entry with a link, or drop the start term and link to the Glossary. Then update in_scope_is_defined_in_the_start_terms_and_the_glossary_with_a_citation and the lead-in.

findings.summary: Soundness: the one-definition test counts only Glossary ids, and the 6-word test removes both copies, so neither test can see the duplicate definition
findings.evidence: each_term_has_one_definition_and_every_term_link_resolves asserts html.matches("<dt id=\"term-{slug}\">").count() == 1, which ignores the `<dt>{term}</dt>` definitions in Words used first. no_run_of_six_words... calls without_definition for both the Glossary and the start-term <dd>, so the verbatim second copy of red and in scope is removed before the comparison. Simpler and correct: count every <dt> whose text is the term across both definition lists and assert it is 1, and compare only the single kept definition against all other text.

findings.summary: The place definition was reworded to slip past the 6-word check, while the same rule is still paraphrased in several places
findings.evidence: The place Glossary entry changed from 'a local-only ship or a scout keeps its place until cleanup' to 'neither a local-only ship nor a scout gives one back before then'. Meanwhile walkthrough[3] ('for a local-only ship or a scout, only cleanup frees it'), t3, t11, limits[6], the counters lead-in and the places-held entry all restate when a place is freed. The run test cannot catch paraphrase. That limit was accepted in the reading, but rewording the definition hides the overlap rather than removing it.

findings.summary: CHANGELOG entry contradicts itself about where terms are defined
findings.evidence: It says the page 'defines yolo, green, red, in scope, places and home once (Words used first and the Glossary)' and that a test 'checks each term has one Glossary entry'. The page defines five of the terms in both sections.

findings.summary: No direct unit test of linked()
findings.evidence: linked() (site.rs:130-151) is exercised only through the real-page tests. A small fixture test for escaping around [[term]] and an unclosed [[ would pin its behavior.

summary: The candidate fixes each finding from the rejected attempt. The overview and failure-list copies are gone, the t2/t11 summaries, glossary entries and t10 trigger now link their terms, and the t10 guard no longer restates red. A new test checks shared 6-word runs, and fmt, clippy and the tests pass (recorded CI, plus my runs of `cargo test -p xtask` and `cargo test -p athena-cap-study`). It still misses the core ask: define each term in exactly one place, the Glossary or Words used first. yolo, green, red, in scope and home are each defined in both sections. red and in scope are word for word identical, and the home entries both say 'a persistent home of its own', so a newcomer still reads the same definitions twice. The new tests hide this: the one-definition test counts only Glossary ids, and the 6-word test removes both copies before it compares. Criterion 2 is therefore unmet, and the verdict is fail. The fix is to keep a single definition per term, link the other section to it, and tighten the tests to count every definition list. I read the page structure from source; the rendered index.html was outside my working directory and reading it was denied.
